## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

\begin{marginfigure}
\mlagentstack{0}{0}{0}{0}{100}{0}
\end{marginfigure}

_Why can an agent that is generating nothing still exhaust the memory of the machine serving it?_

Every token a model reads leaves behind computed state that later tokens attend to, and a serving system keeps that state rather than compute it again. The state occupies accelerator memory in proportion to the context an agent retains, and it occupies that memory for as long as the trajectory lives, including the seconds or minutes the agent spends waiting on a test, a search, or a person. Summed across many concurrent trajectories, this retained state can outweigh the model itself, so the number of agents a machine serves at once is set less by the model than by what the agents keep and how long they keep it. Treating the state as free produces deployments that look well provisioned and then queue, stall, or thrash under real agent traffic. Treating it as disposable throws away work that would have made the next turn cheap. The engineering problem is stewardship of a derived resource, deciding what to share among branches and turns that begin the same way, what to hold through a pause, what to move aside, and what to rebuild on demand. Those decisions live inside the serving system, yet agent builders shape them through the context they send and the waits they create, even on a hosted service they do not operate. In H·S·A terms, this is where State acquires a physical price that grows with Horizon, and that price bounds how much agent work a machine can carry.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Calculate retained attention-state memory and resident fit from model geometry, token count, and storage precision
- Calculate the memory that block allocation and prefix sharing recover from full-cap reservation and duplicated prefixes
- Distinguish compatible, available prefix reuse from the applicability of the underlying information
- Select a chunked-prefill token budget that bounds the gap between output tokens for ongoing requests
- Evaluate keep, move, and recompute policies for paused state against memory pressure and resume latency
- Analyze how residence time converts a memory-fit bound into a sustainable turn rate

:::

## Attention State as a Serving Resource {#sec-vol3-kvcache-introduction}

The connection-pool repair (\ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}) has reached a candidate revision, r18. Its targeted reproducer passes, so the harness submits a fully serialized request of 32,768 tokens and then launches the broader integration test, which takes 45 seconds. Suppose the service keeps the request's attention state on the accelerator throughout that wait. The model generates nothing during the test, yet the retained state occupies memory that another request could use. Keeping it is a service policy, and this chapter prices that policy against its alternatives.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/hsa_locator_s.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="H·S·A locator with the State axis highlighted."}

*State becomes a physical resource claim inside the serving system.*
:::

The tools developed so far stop short of that decision. @Sec-vol3-context-engineering established how the harness selects and refreshes the information in a call, and @sec-vol3-foundation-model-cost priced a cached prefix as a cheaper line on the bill. Neither says how many bytes the computation derived from those tokens occupies, how many trajectories can hold such state at once, or what should happen to it while the agent waits on a tool. Those questions decide whether a node that serves one repair comfortably can serve dozens.

This chapter builds the part of the serving system that manages retained attention state as it is sized, allocated, shared, scheduled, set aside during a pause, and planned for as capacity. Two parties share that work. The application caller controls its submitted context and any cache controls the service exposes. The serving operator controls the allocator, placement, and retention policy. When the two are different organizations, as with a hosted model, the caller influences retention only through the controls the service exposes, and the sections that follow note which party holds each lever.

The chapter follows the state through its life. It first sizes the state a trajectory retains and the pool left once the weights are paid (@sec-vol3-kvcache-geometry). It then shows why reserving each request's largest possible size wastes that pool (@sec-vol3-kvcache-fragmentation) and how fixed-size blocks and shared prefixes recover it (@sec-vol3-kvcache-pagedattention). Reuse across turns comes next, with the conditions a prefix-cache hit must meet (@sec-vol3-kvcache-radix-tree), followed by the scheduling of new prompt work beside ongoing generation (@sec-vol3-kvcache-chunked-prefill) and the choice to keep, move, or drop state during a tool wait (@sec-vol3-kvcache-swapping). The final section turns these mechanisms into a capacity plan, where residence time rather than occupancy alone sets the rate a node sustains (@sec-vol3-kvcache-capacity-planning).

## The Footprint of Retained Attention State {#sec-vol3-kvcache-geometry}

The r18 request's 32,768 tokens do not reach the accelerator as text. In the causal self-attention of the Transformer decoder, each new token attends to earlier tokens through their keys and values [@vaswani2017]. Recomputing those vectors at every decode step would repeat the projections of the whole prefix, so the serving system keeps them.[^fn-kv-memory-bound] @Sec-vol3-foundation-model-autoregressive introduced this stored state; its capacity, sharing, and lifetime are the subject of this chapter.

[^fn-kv-memory-bound]: **Memory-Limited Inference**: Keeping keys and values turns a quadratic recomputation into a memory claim, and that claim soon sets the limit. An analytical study of large-model inference found that sharing one key-value head across all query heads let the same deployment serve contexts more than an order of magnitude longer, because the retained state, not the arithmetic, bounded context length and batch size [@pope2023efficiently]. The rest of this chapter manages that claim. \index{KV cache!memory bound}

::: {#dfn-kv-cache .callout-definition title="KV cache"}

***KV cache***\index{KV cache!definition} is the per-sequence store of attention keys and values that the model has computed for already processed tokens, retained so that later tokens can attend to them without recomputing their projections.

1. **Significance**: Its payload grows linearly with retained tokens, so retained context length, not model size, decides how many sequences share the memory left after the weights.
2. **Distinction**: It is derived computation, not a copy of the prompt text or a summary of it; rebuilding it requires the exact token sequence and a compatible model configuration.
3. **Common pitfall**: Budgeting only the prompt. Every processed output token also adds an entry, so a request's footprint at completion includes its generated tokens.

:::

For a decoder with full causal attention and uniform layer geometry, each retained token contributes a key vector and a value vector at every layer. Let $N_L$ be the number of layers, $H_{\text{KV}}$ the number of key-value heads per layer, $d_{\text{head}}$ the dimension of each head, and $s_{\text{elem}}$ the bytes stored per element. Counting the two vectors gives

$$m_{\text{token}} = 2 \cdot N_L \cdot H_{\text{KV}} \cdot d_{\text{head}} \cdot s_{\text{elem}}$$ {#eq-mem-token}

bytes per retained token. A sequence with KV state for $S$ tokens consequently has payload $M_{\text{KV}} = S \cdot m_{\text{token}}$. Here $S$ counts tokens whose keys and values have actually been computed; a newly sampled token joins $S$ once the model has processed it.

The head count in @eq-mem-token is the number of stored key-value heads, which can be smaller than the number of query heads. Multi-query attention took this to its limit, one key-value head shared by every query head[^fn-mqa-decode-bandwidth] [@shazeer2019fast]. **Grouped-query attention**\index{Grouped-query attention!definition} interpolates between the two: several query heads share one key-value head, dividing the stored head count by the group size relative to a comparable multi-head design [@ainslie2023gqa]. The reduction is fixed when the model is trained; an allocator cannot drop heads from an existing model without changing its computation.

[^fn-mqa-decode-bandwidth]: **Multi-Query Attention**: The motivation was bandwidth before capacity. Incremental decoding reloads every stored key and value at each step, so its speed was bound by memory traffic, and sharing the key-value tensors across heads shrank both the traffic and the stored state at a small cost in quality [@shazeer2019fast]. Grouped-query attention later recovered most of that quality while keeping most of the saving, which is why the head count in @eq-mem-token is a training-time design choice. \index{Multi-query attention!memory bandwidth}

The formula counts tensor payload for full attention over the retained sequence. Allocation granularity, alignment, block metadata, and precision-specific scales add to it, and architectures with local attention or compressed latent state need their own accounting.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: kv-geometry-calc
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ RETAINED ATTENTION STATE: PAYLOAD AND IDEALIZED RESIDENT FIT
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-kvcache-geometry; nbk-05-sizing-the-attention-state-for.
# │ Goal: Derive a token's KV payload and a node's unshared memory-fit bound.
# │ Show: 327,680 bytes/token; 526.0 GB pool; 195/48/12 resident sequences.
# │ How: Registry geometry and capacity, FP16 storage, local runtime reserve.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_memory, fmt_params, fmt_math

class KvGeometry:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ─────────────────────────────────
    _model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    _node = Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100
    n_layers = _model.layers
    n_kv_heads = _model.kv_heads
    d_head = _model.hidden_dim // _model.heads
    element_size = BYTES_FP16
    n_acc = _node.accelerators_per_node
    runtime_reserve = 20 * GB  # scenario: activations and runtime buffers
    ctx_short, ctx_agent, ctx_long = 8_192, 32_768, 131_072  # scenario token counts

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────
    bytes_per_token = calc_kv_cache_size(n_layers, n_kv_heads, d_head, 1, 1, element_size)
    kv_short = bytes_per_token * ctx_short
    kv_agent = bytes_per_token * ctx_agent
    kv_long = bytes_per_token * ctx_long
    node_hbm = n_acc * _node.accelerator.memory.capacity
    weights = _model.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16)
    kv_pool = node_hbm - weights - runtime_reserve
    conc_short = int((kv_pool / kv_short).to("").magnitude)
    conc_agent = int((kv_pool / kv_agent).to("").magnitude)
    conc_long = int((kv_pool / kv_long).to("").magnitude)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────
    check(bytes_per_token.to(byte).magnitude == 327_680, "Registry KV geometry changed")
    check(525.9 < kv_pool.to(GB).magnitude < 526.1, "Expected canonical decimal-GB pool")
    check((conc_short, conc_agent, conc_long) == (195, 48, 12), "Resident-fit bounds changed")
    check(conc_agent * kv_agent <= kv_pool < (conc_agent + 1) * kv_agent, "Floor bound must bracket pool")
    check(kv_long / kv_short == ctx_long / ctx_short, "Payload must scale linearly with retained tokens")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ───────────────────────────────
    params_str = fmt_params(_model.parameters, scale="B", precision=1)
    n_acc_str = fmt_int(n_acc)
    ctx_short_str = fmt_int(ctx_short)
    ctx_agent_str = fmt_int(ctx_agent)
    ctx_long_str = fmt_int(ctx_long)
    kv_short_str = fmt_memory(kv_short, unit=GB, precision=1)
    kv_agent_str = fmt_memory(kv_agent, unit=GB, precision=1)
    kv_long_str = fmt_memory(kv_long, unit=GB, precision=1)
    node_hbm_str = fmt_memory(node_hbm, unit=GB, precision=1)
    weights_str = fmt_memory(weights, unit=GB, precision=1)
    reserve_str = fmt_memory(runtime_reserve, unit=GB, precision=0)
    kv_pool_str = fmt_memory(kv_pool, unit=GB, precision=1)
    conc_short_str = fmt_int(conc_short)
    conc_agent_str = fmt_int(conc_agent)
    conc_long_str = fmt_int(conc_long)
    token_math = fmt_math(
        rf"m_{{\text{{token}}}} = 2 \times {n_layers} \times {n_kv_heads} \times {d_head} \times {element_size.to(byte).magnitude:g} = {bytes_per_token.to(byte).magnitude:,.0f}\;\text{{bytes/token}}"
    )
    trajectory_math = fmt_math(
        rf"M_{{\text{{KV}}}} = {ctx_agent:,} \times {bytes_per_token.to(byte).magnitude:,.0f}\;\text{{bytes}} \approx {kv_agent.to(GB).magnitude:.1f}\;\text{{GB}}"
    )
    pool_math = fmt_math(
        rf"{node_hbm.to(GB).magnitude:.1f} - {weights.to(GB).magnitude:.1f} - {runtime_reserve.to(GB).magnitude:g} \approx {kv_pool.to(GB).magnitude:.1f}\;\text{{GB}}"
    )
    fit_math = fmt_math(rf"\left\lfloor {kv_pool.to(GB).magnitude:.9f} / {kv_agent.to(GB).magnitude:.9f} \right\rfloor = {conc_agent}")
```

The worked estimate uses a representative configuration: the Llama 3 70B model geometry, with `{python} KvGeometry.params_str` parameters, and a DGX H100 node containing `{python} KvGeometry.n_acc_str` accelerators. Both are point-in-time instances; a later model or node changes the inputs, not the arithmetic. Unlike the single-device, 8-bit illustration in @sec-vol3-foundation-model-cost, both weights and KV use 16-bit storage here, with the weights sharded across the node. The memory left after the weights and a runtime reserve is the **KV pool**\index{KV pool!definition}, and the number of sequences whose payload fits in it at once is the **resident-fit bound**\index{Resident-fit bound!definition}. Aggregate arithmetic assumes balanced shards without replicated copies; a deployment must also satisfy each device's limit. @Fig-vol3-context-window-anatomy traces one agent context of this length from its logical zones through that geometry to the number of such contexts the node can hold.

::: {#fig-vol3-context-window-anatomy fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**From Agent Context to KV State**: A 32,768-token agent context (a), divided into system prompt, tool schemas, workspace, turn history, and the latest observation, becomes key and value tensors at every layer (b). The grouped-query model's per-token footprint then sets how many such contexts fit in the node's KV pool, before allocator overhead and headroom." fig-alt="Panel a divides a 32,768-token context into five labeled zones with token counts, grouped as a shared prefix, growing history, and active turn. Arrows lead to panel b, which lists model dimensions, derives 327,680 bytes per token and 10.7 GB per context, and states that resident fit equals the node's KV pool divided by the per-context footprint, so four times the context holds a quarter as many sequences."}
![](images/svg/prompt_context_window_anatomy.svg)
:::

::: {#nbk-05-sizing-the-attention-state-for .callout-notebook title="Sizing the attention state of an agent trajectory"}

**Problem**: The node provides `{python} KvGeometry.node_hbm_str` of aggregate accelerator memory. Its weights occupy `{python} KvGeometry.weights_str`, and this scenario reserves `{python} KvGeometry.reserve_str` for activations and runtime buffers. How many independent, unshared sequences fit in the remaining memory at each of the three context lengths below?

**Math**: The key and value count gives `{python} KvGeometry.token_math`. At the illustrative request length, `{python} KvGeometry.trajectory_math`.

The memory available for KV payload is `{python} KvGeometry.pool_math`. Dividing that pool by a sequence's payload and rounding down gives the resident-fit bound. Using unrounded quantities for the division, the illustrative request gives `{python} KvGeometry.fit_math`. @Tbl-vol3-kv-payload-fit applies the same calculation at three retained lengths.

|         **Retained tokens**         |    **KV payload per sequence**     |        **Sequences that fit**        |
|:-----------------------------------:|:----------------------------------:|:------------------------------------:|
| `{python} KvGeometry.ctx_short_str` | `{python} KvGeometry.kv_short_str` | `{python} KvGeometry.conc_short_str` |
| `{python} KvGeometry.ctx_agent_str` | `{python} KvGeometry.kv_agent_str` | `{python} KvGeometry.conc_agent_str` |
|  `{python} KvGeometry.ctx_long_str` | `{python} KvGeometry.kv_long_str`  | `{python} KvGeometry.conc_long_str`  |

: **Payload and resident fit**: Each sequence stores its own full-attention state; the calculation excludes allocator overhead and additional headroom. {#tbl-vol3-kv-payload-fit tbl-colwidths="[28,38,34]"}

**Systems insight**: Resident fit falls in inverse proportion to retained context. Each fourfold step in length, from `{python} KvGeometry.ctx_short_str` to `{python} KvGeometry.ctx_agent_str` to `{python} KvGeometry.ctx_long_str` tokens, cuts the fit about fourfold while the weights stay fixed. Retained length is therefore the capacity knob, and the harness holds it: keeping every call near its selected working set (principle \ref{pri-vol3-attention-working-set}) keeps a trajectory in the upper rows, while accumulating every observation drives it toward the last. These are payload counts; allocation overhead and headroom lower them, and a rate needs residence time (@sec-vol3-kv-workload-dynamics).

:::

The weights are paid once and shared by every request, while each independent sequence adds its own attention state. Shared prefixes reduce that per-sequence total only where the service retains and safely reuses compatible state.

Architecture and precision change the payload before allocation begins. A model trained to retain fewer key-value heads or compressed latent vectors[^fn-latent-kv-compression] stores less state per token. Lower-precision KV storage shrinks the element payload at the cost of scale overhead and possible output changes, so it needs validation on the intended tasks. Either way, the remaining state still has a lifetime and an owner, and managing those is the rest of this chapter.

[^fn-latent-kv-compression]: **Latent KV Compression**: Multi-head latent attention stores a low-rank latent vector per token and reconstructs per-head keys and values from it during attention, trading extra projection arithmetic for a much smaller cache [@deepseek2024v2]. It changes $m_{\text{token}}$ in @eq-mem-token but none of the lifetime questions that follow: a latent cache is still allocated, shared, paused, and evicted as blocks. \index{Multi-head latent attention!KV footprint}

For the repair agent, retaining state during the integration test is one such lifetime decision. The caller may prefer a faster resume, while the operator must weigh that benefit against competing requests. Before comparing those policies, the allocator must turn the payload estimate into actual storage. Reserving every sequence's largest possible future size can waste the pool well before its useful tensor contents reach capacity.

## Memory Fragmentation {#sec-vol3-kvcache-fragmentation}

The repair agent's next request can grow when the integration test returns a log. The serving operator must provide space for that additional KV state without knowing the final length of every concurrent request. The footprint calculation gives the bytes needed for tokens already processed. An allocation policy determines how much additional memory is reserved, whether a growing request must move, and when released capacity can serve another request.

### Reservation and growth

The simplest policy, **static reservation**\index{Static reservation!definition}, allocates a contiguous buffer for the configured token cap at admission. The request then grows within its cap without reallocating, and the unused remainder of the buffer is unavailable to every other request for as long as the reservation lives. The reservation covers KV capacity only; activations and runtime buffers draw on separate memory.

```{python}
#| label: kv-static-reservation-calc
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ STATIC RESERVATION
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-kvcache-fragmentation reservation example.
# │ Goal: Separate final-length utilization from a resident-fit bound.
# │ Show: Final-length efficiency of 6.25 percent; 48 full-cap reservations.
# │ How: Registry model and node, local cap/mean and runtime reserve assumptions.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_memory, fmt_percent
from mlsysim.physics.agents import calc_kv_cache_bytes_per_token

class StaticReservation:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
    model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    node = Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100
    elem_size = BYTES_FP16
    runtime_reserve = 20 * GB  # scenario: node-wide activations/runtime reserve
    s_max = 32_768  # illustrative deployment cap, not a model specification
    mean_final_tokens = 2_048  # hypothetical mean FINAL length, not a trace mean

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    bytes_per_token = calc_kv_cache_bytes_per_token(model, bytes_per_elem=elem_size)
    node_hbm = node.accelerators_per_node * node.accelerator.memory.capacity
    weights = model.size_in_bytes(elem_size)
    pool = node_hbm - weights - runtime_reserve
    reservation = s_max * bytes_per_token
    reservations = int((pool / reservation).to("").magnitude)
    efficiency = mean_final_tokens / s_max
    mean_doubled = 2 * mean_final_tokens  # checkpoint variation on the same scenario

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(pool.to(byte).magnitude > 0, "The KV pool must be positive")
    check(mean_doubled <= s_max, "The checkpoint variation must respect the cap")
    check(reservations * reservation <= pool < (reservations + 1) * reservation, "The count must be the whole-reservation fit bound")
    check(0 < mean_final_tokens <= s_max, "Final lengths must respect the cap")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    s_max_str = fmt_int(s_max)
    mean_final_tokens_str = fmt_int(mean_final_tokens)
    pool_gb_str = fmt_memory(pool, unit=GB, precision=1)
    reservation_gb_str = fmt_memory(reservation, unit=GB, precision=2)
    reservations_str = fmt_int(reservations)
    efficiency_str = fmt_percent(efficiency, precision=2, style="prose")
    mean_doubled_str = fmt_int(mean_doubled)
```

In the same `{python} StaticReservation.pool_gb_str` KV pool, a cap of `{python} StaticReservation.s_max_str` tokens requires `{python} StaticReservation.reservation_gb_str` per reservation. Dividing the pool by that reservation and rounding down gives `{python} StaticReservation.reservations_str` resident reservations, assuming balanced sharding and no additional overhead outside the stated reserve.

Suppose the request population finishes at a hypothetical mean length of `{python} StaticReservation.mean_final_tokens_str` tokens. Each reservation is then only `{python} StaticReservation.efficiency_str` populated even at completion, `{python} StaticReservation.mean_final_tokens_str` of `{python} StaticReservation.s_max_str` slots, and less while a request is still growing. Measured systems show the same pattern. In the serving systems profiled when paged KV allocation was introduced, only 20.4 to 38.2 percent of KV memory held actual token state, with the rest lost to reservation slack and fragmentation [@kwon2023vllm].

A second policy grows a contiguous allocation as tokens arrive. When adjacent capacity is unavailable, the allocator obtains a larger buffer, copies the initialized entries, and releases the old one, holding both allocations during the copy. Contiguous here means one range in the allocator's address space. Accelerators translate addresses in hardware, so the restriction comes from an allocator and attention kernel that require each sequence's KV tensor to occupy one such range.

### Two kinds of unused capacity

Unused slots inside a reservation are **internal fragmentation**\index{Internal fragmentation!definition}; free capacity split into extents too small for a contiguous request is **external fragmentation**\index{External fragmentation!definition}. The distinction comes from storage allocation for multiprogrammed computers[^fn-fragmentation-internal-external] [@randell1969fragmentation]. @Tbl-vol3-kv-fragmentation-taxonomies separates them because each has a different remedy: releasing slack cures the first, and changing the allocation granularity cures the second.

| **Condition**          | **Where capacity is unavailable**                           | **Consequence**                                                               |
|:-----------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Internal fragmentation | Inside an allocation, beyond its initialized entries        | Other requests cannot use the reserved slots                                  |
| External fragmentation | In separate free extents of a variable-size allocation pool | A contiguous request can fail even when aggregate free capacity is sufficient |

: **Unused KV capacity**: Reservation slack belongs to an allocation; external fragmentation concerns free space that cannot satisfy a particular contiguous request. {#tbl-vol3-kv-fragmentation-taxonomies tbl-colwidths="[22,40,38]"}

[^fn-fragmentation-internal-external]: **Internal and External Fragmentation**: The analysis of storage allocation that named the two losses also measured their trade: rounding requests up to fewer standard sizes cost more storage in internal fragmentation than it recovered in external fragmentation [@randell1969fragmentation]. Paged KV allocation makes the same trade on purpose, accepting at most one partial block per sequence in exchange for a pool in which any free block fits any request. \index{Fragmentation!internal versus external}

For a concrete external-fragmentation example, suppose an allocator has three free extents of exactly 256 token slots each, separated by live allocations. A request requiring 512 contiguous slots cannot fit in any extent, although the free extents together have sufficient capacity. The failure comes from the contiguity requirement, not from a shortage of memory.

In the repair workload, the paused trajectory keeps its allocation under the chapter's initial retention policy while other requests need to grow. An operator therefore needs two mechanisms: a space-efficient allocation unit, which fixed-size blocks provide, and an explicit lifetime policy, which @sec-vol3-kvcache-swapping develops.

## Paged KV Allocation {#sec-vol3-kvcache-pagedattention}

When the integration-test log extends the repair context, the serving engine need not relocate the entire existing KV tensor. It can allocate additional fixed-size blocks and add their identifiers to the request's block table. The attention kernel follows that table when reading earlier token positions. PagedAttention demonstrated this combination of block allocation and attention over noncontiguous KV storage [@kwon2023vllm]. Its lineage is paged virtual memory, which the Atlas one-level store introduced to decouple a program's contiguous address space from scattered physical frames [@kilburn1962onelevel]. The block table applies the same indirection to token positions, so a sequence can grow without a contiguous extent.

::: {#dfn-paged-kv-cache .callout-definition title="Paged KV block table"}

***Paged KV block table***\index{Paged attention!definition}\index{Paged KV block table|see{Paged attention}}\index{KV cache!block table} is a per-sequence software mapping from logical token blocks to the physical KV blocks that store their initialized key and value entries.

1. **Significance**: A sequence can grow by acquiring another block without relocating its existing blocks.
2. **Distinction**: The table maps token positions for the attention kernel; it is not the accelerator's hardware page table.
3. **Common pitfall**: A mapped block has allocated capacity, but only its initialized token entries may be read as valid KV state.

:::

### Mapping tokens to blocks

Consider an illustrative block size of four tokens, chosen to make the mapping visible rather than to recommend a production setting. A ten-token prefix occupies logical blocks 0, 1, and 2. Its block table is `[3, 7, 9]`: positions 0–3 reside in physical block 3, positions 4–7 in block 7, and positions 8–9 in the first two slots of block 9. Physical IDs are labels in the allocator's pool, not token positions or memory addresses.

For any token position, the kernel identifies its logical block by integer division by the block size, uses the table to find the physical block, and selects the token's offset by taking the remainder. Thus position 9 selects logical block 2, physical block 9, and slot 1. The actual address also depends on the layer, KV head, and tensor layout. This software lookup preserves logical sequence order even when physical block IDs are scattered. @Fig-vol3-pagedattention-mapping traces the ten-token example through the table into the pool, and previews the copy-on-write step that prefix sharing requires.

::: {#fig-vol3-pagedattention-mapping fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Block Table Indirection and Tail Copy-on-Write**: Panel (a) follows each logical block through its table entry to a physical block scattered among other requests' blocks; position 9 resolves to logical block 2, then to physical block 9, slot 1. Panel (b) shows two candidates that share the full blocks 3 and 7, while candidate B's private append first copies the two initialized entries of the shared tail into block 14." fig-alt="Panel a shows three logical blocks of four slots holding positions 0 to 9, arrows to a block table with entries 3, 7, and 9, and elbow arrows to physical blocks 3, 7, and 9 in a row of twelve blocks, some used by other requests. A card shows the lookup for position 9. Panel b shows candidate A's table 3, 7, 9 and candidate B's table 3, 7, 14, shared blocks 3 and 7 with two owners, and an arrow copying slots from block 9 into block 14, where position 10 is written."}
![](images/svg/paged_attention_virtual_memory.svg)
:::

Within a pool of interchangeable fixed-size blocks, any free block satisfies a new block request, so paging removes external fragmentation at the block granularity. The remaining waste is metadata, temporary buffers, and the unused slots of each sequence's final block.

### Block size and tail waste

The final block may contain uninitialized slots, the **tail waste**\index{Tail waste!definition} $\Delta_{\text{tail}}$. If a block holds $p$ tokens, $0 \leq \Delta_{\text{tail}} \leq p-1$, with a mean of $(p-1)/2$ when sequence lengths have uniformly distributed remainders modulo $p$; a length divisible by $p$ wastes nothing.

Smaller blocks reduce this tail bound and allow finer-grained sharing and copying. They also require more table entries for the same context and more block-management work. Larger blocks reverse those tendencies and may suit a kernel's access pattern better. The appropriate size depends on the length distribution, branching behavior, and kernel.

```{python}
#| label: lego-05-physical-block-sizing
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PHYSICAL BLOCK SIZING
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: notebook nbk-05-sizing-physical-blocks-for-a.
# │ Goal: Convert allocation granularity into physical storage and a tail bound.
# │ Show: Node-wide block footprints and maximum tail slack for 16/64 tokens.
# │ How: Registry model geometry and precision; explicitly hypothetical sizes.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_memory, fmt_percent
from mlsysim.physics.agents import calc_kv_cache_bytes_per_token

class PhysicalBlockSizing:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
    model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    elem_size = BYTES_FP16
    small_tokens, large_tokens = 16, 64  # illustrative allocator choices
    ctx_agent = KvGeometry.ctx_agent  # scenario agent context from the footprint estimate

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    bytes_per_token = calc_kv_cache_bytes_per_token(model, bytes_per_elem=elem_size)
    small_block = small_tokens * bytes_per_token
    large_block = large_tokens * bytes_per_token
    small_tail_tokens = small_tokens - 1
    large_tail_tokens = large_tokens - 1
    small_tail = small_tail_tokens * bytes_per_token
    large_tail = large_tail_tokens * bytes_per_token
    large_tail_share = large_tail_tokens / ctx_agent  # worst-case tail share of one agent context

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(0 * byte <= small_tail < small_block, "Tail must fit inside one block")
    check(0 * byte <= large_tail < large_block, "Tail must fit inside one block")
    check(small_block * large_tokens == large_block * small_tokens, "Both block sizes must use the same KV geometry")
    check(large_tail_share < 0.005, "Prose claims the worst tail is a fraction of a percent at agent length")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    bytes_per_token_str = fmt_memory(bytes_per_token, unit=byte, precision=0)
    small_tokens_str = fmt_int(small_tokens)
    large_tokens_str = fmt_int(large_tokens)
    small_block_mb_str = fmt_memory(small_block, unit=MB, precision=2)
    large_block_mb_str = fmt_memory(large_block, unit=MB, precision=2)
    small_tail_tokens_str = fmt_int(small_tail_tokens)
    large_tail_tokens_str = fmt_int(large_tail_tokens)
    small_tail_mb_str = fmt_memory(small_tail, unit=MB, precision=2)
    large_tail_mb_str = fmt_memory(large_tail, unit=MB, precision=2)
    ctx_agent_str = fmt_int(ctx_agent)
    large_tail_share_str = fmt_percent(large_tail_share, precision=1, style="prose")
```

::: {#nbk-05-sizing-physical-blocks-for-a .callout-notebook title="Converting block size into KV storage"}

**Problem**: With the same Llama 3 70B geometry and 16-bit KV representation, what storage granularity and maximum tail slack follow from two different block sizes?

**Math**: Each token requires `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.bytes_per_token_str` across all model layers and heads. Multiplying that footprint by `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.small_tokens_str` tokens gives `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.small_block_mb_str` per block. Multiplying by `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.large_tokens_str` instead gives `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.large_block_mb_str`. These are aggregate footprints across the model's shards, not the allocation on each accelerator.

The maximum unused tail has one fewer slot than a full block. The smaller block can therefore leave `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.small_tail_tokens_str` slots, or `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.small_tail_mb_str`, unused; the larger can leave `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.large_tail_tokens_str` slots, or `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.large_tail_mb_str`, unused.

Against a `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.ctx_agent_str`-token agent context, even the larger block's worst tail is `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.large_tail_share_str` of the sequence's state.

**Systems insight**: Tail slack is at most one block per unshared sequence, so its share falls as the sequence grows. At agent context lengths, tail waste stops being the deciding term: choose the block size for kernel efficiency and sharing granularity, and revisit tail waste only for workloads dominated by short sequences.

:::

```{python}
#| label: kv-paged-waste-calc
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PAGED ALLOCATION PAYOFF
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-kvcache-pagedattention, paragraph after
# │          nbk-05-sizing-physical-blocks-for-a.
# │ Goal: Answer the static-reservation count with what paging admits under a
# │       stated length distribution.
# │ Show: 0.4 percent tail waste at 16-token blocks, 1.5 percent at 64;
# │       780 paged sequences vs. 48 full-cap reservations (about 16x).
# │ How: calc_expected_paged_kv_tokens over a capped-exponential length model
# │      (modeling assumption) with StaticReservation's mean, cap, and pool.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.physics.memory import calc_expected_paged_kv_tokens
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_percent, fmt_multiple

class PagedWaste:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
    block_small = PhysicalBlockSizing.small_tokens
    block_large = PhysicalBlockSizing.large_tokens
    mean_tokens = StaticReservation.mean_final_tokens  # same hypothetical mean final length
    s_max = StaticReservation.s_max
    bytes_per_token = StaticReservation.bytes_per_token
    pool = StaticReservation.pool

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    alloc_small, frag_small = calc_expected_paged_kv_tokens(mean_tokens, s_max, block_small)
    alloc_large, frag_large = calc_expected_paged_kv_tokens(mean_tokens, s_max, block_large)
    fit_paged = int((pool / (alloc_small * bytes_per_token)).to("").magnitude)
    gain = fit_paged / StaticReservation.reservations

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(0 < frag_small < frag_large < 0.02, "Larger blocks must waste more, and both only a few percent")
    check(mean_tokens <= alloc_small < mean_tokens + block_small, "Expected allocation exceeds the mean by less than one block")
    check(fit_paged == 780, "Paged fit on the canonical pool changed")
    check(15 < gain < 17, "Prose claims about sixteen times as many sequences")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    frag_small_str = fmt_percent(frag_small, precision=1, style="prose")
    frag_large_str = fmt_percent(frag_large, precision=1, style="prose")
    fit_paged_str = fmt_int(fit_paged)
    gain_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(gain))  # prose says "roughly"
```

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/kv_paged_vs_static_margin.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Two horizontal bars on one linear scale: a short gray bar labeled 48 for full-cap reservation and a long green bar labeled 780 for paged blocks, with the note sequences resident, same pool."}

*Allocating blocks as tokens arrive admits about `{python} PagedWaste.gain_mult_str` the sequences of full-cap reservation.*
:::

The tail bounds become an expected waste once a length distribution is stated. Model final lengths as exponential with the hypothetical mean of `{python} StaticReservation.mean_final_tokens_str` tokens, capped at the `{python} StaticReservation.s_max_str`-token limit used for static reservation. Under that assumption, `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.small_tokens_str`-token blocks leave `{python} PagedWaste.frag_small_str` of allocated KV memory unused and `{python} PhysicalBlockSizing.large_tokens_str`-token blocks leave `{python} PagedWaste.frag_large_str`. Dividing the pool that admitted `{python} StaticReservation.reservations_str` full-cap reservations by the expected paged allocation gives about `{python} PagedWaste.fit_paged_str` sequences, roughly `{python} PagedWaste.gain_mult_str` as many. That is the payoff of paging. Allocation tracks the tokens a sequence has actually produced rather than the cap it might reach. The count is a mean under the stated length model; the resident count fluctuates with the lengths actually present.

### Sharing a prefix without sharing its future writes

```{python}
#| label: kv-fork-copy-calc
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ FORK COST UNDER CONTIGUOUS ALLOCATION
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-kvcache-pagedattention, prefix-sharing paragraph.
# │ Goal: Size the tensor copy that block sharing avoids when candidates fork.
# │ Show: 10.7 GB copied for four candidates of an 8,192-token prefix.
# │ How: Registry KV geometry (PhysicalBlockSizing); scenario prefix and fan-out.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_memory

class ForkCopy:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
    prefix_tokens = 8_192  # scenario: processed prefix shared by the candidates
    branches = 4  # scenario: sampled candidate repairs
    bytes_per_token = PhysicalBlockSizing.bytes_per_token

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    copied = branches * prefix_tokens * bytes_per_token

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(branches == 4, "Prose spells out four candidates")
    check(10 < copied.to(GB).magnitude < 11, "Prose describes roughly ten gigabytes copied")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    prefix_str = fmt_int(prefix_tokens)
    copied_str = fmt_memory(copied, unit=GB, precision=1)
```

Deliberation that samples several candidates to buy evidence (principle \ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}) makes forks routine. Candidate repairs can begin from the same processed prefix and then generate different continuations. Their block tables may refer to the same immutable prefix blocks if the model computation is compatible and the service permits sharing. The saving is large at agent context lengths. A contiguous allocator that deep-copies an `{python} ForkCopy.prefix_str`-token prefix into four candidates writes `{python} ForkCopy.copied_str` of KV state for the Llama 3 70B geometry, while block-table duplication copies none of that payload. The runtime still constructs or shares metadata and records ownership; copying a block table and updating its references can require work proportional to its number of entries.

The partial tail needs special treatment. Two candidates cannot independently append into the same shared writable slot. In the ten-token example, both candidates initially refer to `[3, 7, 9]`. Before candidate B writes position 10, the runtime allocates block 14, copies the two initialized entries from block 9, and redirects B's last table entry. The write then occurs at slot 2 of block 14. This **copy-on-write**\index{Copy-on-write!KV tail}[^fn-cow-tenex-pages] operation leaves candidate A's state unchanged. @Tbl-vol3-kv-cow-trace follows the ownership change; its counts assume these two candidates are the only owners.

| **State**                     | **Candidate A table** | **Candidate B table** | **Physical ownership**                                   |
|:------------------------------|:----------------------|:----------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------|
| Before append                 | `[3, 7, 9]`           | `[3, 7, 9]`           | Blocks 3, 7, and 9 each have two owners                  |
| After B's private-tail append | `[3, 7, 9]`           | `[3, 7, 14]`          | Blocks 3 and 7 retain two owners; 9 and 14 each have one |

: **Partial-tail copy-on-write**: Full prefix blocks remain shared while the initialized portion of the tail is copied before a private append. The block IDs label allocations; they do not imply contiguous addresses. {#tbl-vol3-kv-cow-trace tbl-colwidths="[23,20,20,37]"}

[^fn-cow-tenex-pages]: **Copy-on-Write**: The TENEX time-sharing system of the early 1970s gave each page a status bit that let processes share large parts of an address space and obtain private copies of only the pages they changed [@bobrow1972tenex]. Forked candidates reuse the idea at block granularity, which is why a fan-out of sampled repairs costs private blocks in proportion to what each candidate writes, not to the prefix they share. \index{Copy-on-write!TENEX origin}

This is different from appending at a full-block boundary. After a twelve-token prefix in four-token blocks, position 12 starts a new logical block. The appending candidate acquires a fresh block; it does not copy an old tail. A private partial tail can likewise accept another entry without a copy. The necessary operation depends on both the fill level and ownership of the block being modified.

When a candidate is discarded, its references are released, and a block returns to the free pool once no owner needs its contents and no in-flight reader or writer still accesses it. Reference counts and completion signals from outstanding device operations enforce both conditions. A dormant prefix-cache entry can keep a block alive after every active request has released it, which is the subject of the next section. Physical storage is therefore the count of unique blocks, not the sum of logical bytes across candidates.

::: {#chk-05-memory-fragmentation .callout-checkpoint title="Reasoning about KV allocation"}

The allocation policy must preserve each sequence's state while managing capacity shared by many requests.

- [ ] **Reservation estimate**: If the hypothetical mean final length doubled to `{python} StaticReservation.mean_doubled_str` tokens under the same `{python} StaticReservation.s_max_str`-token cap, what fraction of each static reservation would be populated at completion, and would static reservation admit any more sequences?
- [ ] **External fragmentation**: Can you identify why the three free extents in the example cannot satisfy its contiguous request, and why a fixed-size block pool changes that condition?
- [ ] **Tail ownership**: Can you trace a private append to a shared partial tail and distinguish it from an append at a full-block boundary?
- [ ] **Reclamation**: Can you explain why ending an active request does not always make its blocks immediately reusable?

:::

Block allocation separates logical sequence growth from the placement of its KV state. Sharing then allows compatible candidates to use one physical copy of their common history. Reuse across later model calls needs an additional mechanism: the service must find compatible state that remains available and decide whether retaining it is worthwhile. That is the role of prefix caching.

## Prefix Caching Across Turns {#sec-vol3-kvcache-radix-tree}

In the connection-pool repair, the call that reads the integration-test result may begin with the same instructions, tool definitions, and earlier observations as the preceding call. If the service retained the corresponding KV state, it can attach that state to the new request and prefill only the remaining input. @Sec-vol3-foundation-model-cost priced this saving as prefix caching; here it becomes a serving mechanism with an index, an ownership rule, and an eviction policy.

::: {#dfn-prefix-cache .callout-definition title="Prefix cache"}

***Prefix cache***\index{Prefix cache!definition} is the serving system's index of retained KV state, keyed by exact token prefix and computation configuration, from which a later request with the same beginning attaches state instead of prefilling it.

1. **Significance**: It converts repeated prefill into a lookup across request boundaries. The saving per turn grows with the matched prefix length and recurs at every turn whose prefix survives, which is why a stable prefix layout pays across a whole trajectory.
2. **Distinction**: Block sharing reuses state among candidates forked from one computation; a prefix cache finds reusable state for requests that arrive independently, and it keeps that state only as long as its eviction policy allows.
3. **Common pitfall**: Reading a hit as a freshness check. A hit says that the tokens and configuration match, not that the information they encode is still current.

:::

### Compatibility before reuse

For the causal full-attention model used here, reusable state corresponds to an exact input prefix, not a passage with similar meaning. Matching token IDs is only the first test: the state must also belong to compatible model weights, adapters, positions, attention masks, and other computation settings. Where an input contains images or other nontext data, matching placeholder tokens is insufficient; the underlying model inputs must match as well. A serving system must identify these dependencies in its cache key or otherwise enforce them before reuse.

Compatibility, availability, and permission answer different questions. Compatible tensors may have been evicted or may require a transfer before they can be used. Available tensors may belong to a different isolation domain, such as another tenant whose state must stay private, and therefore be ineligible for sharing. The reusable prefix is the longest one that satisfies all three conditions, which can be shorter than the longest string found in an index. Generated tokens qualify only after their corresponding KV state has actually been computed and retained.

These conditions are also separate from whether an observation remains appropriate for the task. Changing the repository from r17 to r18 does not alter tensors already computed for an unchanged prompt describing r17. Those tensors may remain numerically compatible with that old prompt even though the prompt no longer supplies the evidence needed to judge r18. The selection policy in @sec-vol3-context-engineering determines which evidence to include. Once the caller refreshes or replaces that evidence in the serialized input, prefix matching stops at the first changed token, and freshness is restored by the input rather than by the cache.

### Finding usable prefix state

A **radix prefix cache**\index{Radix prefix cache!definition} indexes token sequences with a compressed prefix tree,[^fn-radix-patricia-trie] whose edges may represent several tokens rather than one. Following matching edges from the root identifies a common prefix and the associated KV storage [@zheng2024sglang]. The service must then obtain usable ownership of that storage before eviction can reclaim it. Lookup cost grows with the length of the request prefix it examines. A hash index of blocks keyed by their contents and preceding prefix supports the same reuse contract.

[^fn-radix-patricia-trie]: **Compressed Prefix Tree**: The trie stored one symbol per edge, so a shared prefix was found by walking from the root [@fredkin1960]. PATRICIA collapsed chains of single-child nodes into one edge, so index size grows with the number of stored keys rather than their length [@morrison1968patricia]. The same compression matters for KV reuse, because agent prefixes run to thousands of tokens and a one-token-per-edge index would spend a node on each of them. \index{Radix tree!PATRICIA origin}

The match must extend from the beginning of the input. A repeated passage after a changed earlier token is not, in general, reusable as an independent suffix: its attention state was computed under a different preceding context. This is the physical consequence of the stable-prefix layout in @sec-vol3-context-engineering-staging. Keeping volatile fields later preserves more opportunities for reuse, while rewriting an earlier region shortens the common prefix. Compaction that rewrites only a later region keeps the prefix before it.

Block boundaries create a policy choice without changing what compatibility means. Return to the illustrative ten-token prefix in four-token blocks `[3, 7, 9]`. The two full blocks hold eight tokens, and block `9` holds two initialized entries. A service that supports partial-tail reuse can preserve all ten tokens and copy those two entries to a private tail before a divergent append, as in the preceding sharing example. A service that caches only complete blocks instead reuses eight tokens and prefills the remaining two. Both policies are correct: one pays for tail handling, the other repeats a small amount of computation.

### Retention and eviction under pressure

A finished request releases its active claim on KV state while the cache may keep its own claim, so dormant cached blocks remain occupied storage in case another request reuses them. The service's retention policy decides whether the next turn finds that state ready, must restore it, or must recompute it.

Reuse and reclamation must respect ownership. Before using a hit, the service acquires the references needed by the new request. Before recycling a block, it removes the cache's claim, confirms that no other owner needs the block, and waits for outstanding device operations that could access it to finish; a zero active-request count is only the first of these checks. Index updates and ownership changes must also prevent a lookup from acquiring a block while that block is being reclaimed.

A useful radix-cache policy, **leaf-first eviction**\index{Leaf-first eviction!definition}, retains complete paths from the root and evicts unused leaves first. Removing a leaf preserves its shared ancestors for other requests; an ancestor becomes a candidate once no retained descendants require that path. Least-recently-used selection among eligible leaves is one concrete policy [@zheng2024sglang], a bet that recent use predicts future reuse.[^fn-lru-belady-optimal] @Fig-vol3-radix-tree-cache shows the cascade: a dormant node with a cached child is not yet eligible, and evicting that child makes it a leaf that is.

::: {#fig-vol3-radix-tree-cache fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Leaf-First Eviction in a Radix Prefix Cache**: Each node stands for a run of tokens and the KV blocks that hold them, so a request's cached state is the path from the root to its node. Nodes on a running request's path stay active. Only dormant leaves are eligible, which is why the dormant Other-task node in panel (a) survives until its Final-turn child is evicted in panel (b). A least-recently-used policy would choose among the eligible leaves; it never removes an ancestor before its retained descendants." fig-alt="Two copies of a three-level tree. Panel a has an active shared-prefix root, an active repair-history node with an active test-log-turn leaf and a dormant rejected-branch leaf, and a dormant other-task node with a dormant final-turn leaf; the two dormant leaves are shaded as eligible for eviction. Panel b shows the final-turn leaf faded as evicted and the other-task node now shaded as an eligible dormant leaf. A legend defines active, dormant, eligible, and evicted."}
![](images/svg/radix_prefix_tree_architecture.svg)
:::

[^fn-lru-belady-optimal]: **Replacement with Foresight**: The classic study of page replacement showed that the optimal policy evicts the page whose next use lies furthest in the future, a rule no online system can apply because it needs the future reference string [@belady1966study]. Recency-based policies approximate it. An agent harness sometimes holds part of that future, such as a tool launch that will idle a prefix for minutes, which is why a retention hint from the caller can beat recency alone. \index{Belady optimal replacement!prefix cache}

This prefix-closed residency rule is a serving simplification. Freeing a prefix block leaves a retained suffix block's values intact, but the next full-attention step needs the complete preceding state, so an orphaned suffix is unusable until the missing prefix is restored or recomputed from its inputs.

Retention therefore trades occupied capacity against the work a future hit would avoid. Recency is imperfect evidence: a recently created speculative branch may never run again, while an older shared prefix may serve many requests. A better eviction score weighs expected reuse times reconstruction cost against uniquely reclaimable storage, and the workload sets the weights.

### Measuring reuse and exposing the contract

Potential token matches overstate the benefit when state is unavailable, sharing is disallowed, or the service rounds reuse down to a block boundary. Measure tokens actually served from reusable KV state. Over a specified set of requests, define the **token-weighted prefix hit rate**\index{Prefix hit rate!definition} as

$$\rho_{\text{prefix}} = \frac{\sum_{i} S_{\text{match}}^{(i)}}{\sum_{i} S_{\text{prompt}}^{(i)}}$$ {#eq-hprefix}

Here $S_{\text{prompt}}^{(i)}$ is the number of prompt tokens in request $i$, and $S_{\text{match}}^{(i)}$ counts the prompt tokens whose compatible KV state the request actually reuses, after availability, permission, and boundary restrictions. The denominator includes all prompt tokens in the same request set. In the full-block-only policy above, the reused count is eight, not the ten-token potential match. A service should distinguish reuse that requires restoration from reuse already resident on the accelerator.

```{python}
#| label: kv-prefix-hit-savings-calc
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ WHAT A PREFIX HIT AVOIDS
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-kvcache-radix-tree, "Measuring reuse" paragraph.
# │ Goal: Put a number on the prefill work a prefix hit avoids.
# │ Show: 1.34 GB of state; ~578 + ~22 trillion operations; ~169 ms at the
# │       sustained rate; ~5 ms weight-read floor for a short suffix pass.
# │ How: Registry model/node; linear 2NS plus causal attention 2LdS^2
# │      (@eq-appdx-prefill-long); sustained rate = node peak x MfuHigh x 0.9.
# │ Note: ChunkedIteration and PausedStateChoice reuse sustained_rate.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_memory, fmt_percent, MarkdownStr

class PrefixHit:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
    model = Models.Language.Llama3_70B
    node = Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100
    prefix_tokens = 4_096  # scenario: invariant instructions and tool schemas
    suffix_tokens = 32  # scenario: short novel suffix appended after a hit
    utilization = Literature.Training.MfuHigh * 0.9  # scenario: sustained prefill utilization

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_params = model.parameters.to("count").magnitude
    bytes_per_token = PhysicalBlockSizing.bytes_per_token
    state = prefix_tokens * bytes_per_token
    linear_ops = 2 * n_params * prefix_tokens * flop
    attention_ops = 2 * model.layers * model.hidden_dim * prefix_tokens**2 * flop
    sustained_rate = node.accelerators_per_node * node.accelerator.compute.peak_flops * utilization
    t_rebuild = ((linear_ops + attention_ops) / sustained_rate).to(ms)
    weights = model.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16)
    node_bw = node.accelerators_per_node * node.accelerator.memory.bandwidth
    t_weight_read = (weights / node_bw).to(ms)
    t_suffix_ops = (2 * n_params * suffix_tokens * flop / sustained_rate).to(ms)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(attention_ops < linear_ops, "Weight work must dominate at this prefix length")
    check(t_suffix_ops < t_weight_read, "A short suffix pass must sit below the ridge (weight-read bound)")
    check(150 < t_rebuild.magnitude < 190, "Prose describes roughly 170 ms of avoided prefill")
    check(t_weight_read < t_rebuild / 10, "The suffix floor must be far below the avoided prefill")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    prefix_str = fmt_int(prefix_tokens)
    suffix_str = fmt_int(suffix_tokens)
    state_str = fmt_memory(state, unit=GB, precision=2)
    linear_str = fmt_int(linear_ops.to(flop).magnitude / 1e12)
    attention_str = fmt_int(attention_ops.to(flop).magnitude / 1e12)
    utilization_str = fmt_percent(utilization, precision=0, style="prose")
    rate_str = fmt_int(sustained_rate.to(TFLOPs / second).magnitude)
    rebuild_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_int(t_rebuild.magnitude)} ms")
    weight_read_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_int(t_weight_read.magnitude)} ms")
```

What a hit is worth follows from the same geometry. Suppose the repair agent's invariant instructions and tool schemas form a `{python} PrefixHit.prefix_str`-token prefix. Its KV state occupies `{python} PrefixHit.state_str` across the node. Reconstructing that state takes about `{python} PrefixHit.linear_str` trillion weight operations plus about `{python} PrefixHit.attention_str` trillion for causal attention (@eq-appdx-prefill-long). If the node sustains `{python} PrefixHit.utilization_str` of its peak 16-bit rate, about `{python} PrefixHit.rate_str` trillion operations per second, that is roughly `{python} PrefixHit.rebuild_str` of prefill on every turn that misses. A turn that hits and appends a `{python} PrefixHit.suffix_str`-token suffix still makes one pass over the weights. A pass that short has too few tokens for arithmetic to dominate, so reading the weights once bounds it at about `{python} PrefixHit.weight_read_str` (@eq-appdx-batched-step). Across a trajectory of many turns, the avoided prefill repeats at every turn whose prefix survives.

The hit rate in @eq-hprefix measures avoided reconstruction of prompt state. Elapsed time also includes the new suffix's prefill, output generation, queueing, and transfers, any of which can dominate after a hit. A falling hit rate warrants checking both sides of the interface: changes in serialization can shorten matches, while retention pressure, placement, or a configuration change can make matching state unavailable or incompatible.

For a hosted service, the caller needs an explicit reuse contract rather than assumptions about the hidden allocator: eligible inputs and configurations, sharing boundaries, supported cache hints or retention lifetimes, and what the reported cached-token count means. Expiration couples that contract to tool waits. If a tool runs longer than the service's idle lifetime for cached state, the next turn finds no reusable prefix and pays the full prefill, which is the hosted form of the drop policy in @sec-vol3-kvcache-swapping. A harness that knows a wait will outlast that lifetime plans for the miss instead of discovering it in latency. The count the provider reports is the caller's main instrument, and it answers a narrower question than it appears to.

::: {#psp-05-reading-a-cached-token-count .callout-perspective title="Reading a cached-token count"}

A usage record that reports cached input tokens states how many of this request's prompt tokens the provider served from reusable state, which is the numerator of @eq-hprefix for one request as the provider measured it. It is silent on where the tensors resided, how they were indexed, and how long they will survive.

Its diagnostic value comes from its trajectory across turns. Divided by prompt tokens, it gives the caller's own hit rate. A count that falls to zero after a long tool wait points to expiration. A count that settles at a stable but shorter value points to a change early in the serialized input, because matching stops at the first changed token, and that cause the caller can fix in its own layout.

:::

The application must remain correct on a cache miss, because the selected context, not the cache, supplies the model input. A hit removes repeated work only; a large test log or retrieved observation still brings new prefill, and scheduling that prefill alongside ongoing generation is the next problem.

## Chunked Prefill Scheduling {#sec-vol3-kvcache-chunked-prefill}

Prefix reuse avoids processing an unchanged prefix, but a new observation still introduces work. When the repair agent submits selected integration-test output, the serving engine must process the uncached part of the serialized request before producing its response. Other requests may already be generating tokens on the same accelerators. If the engine runs the entire new prefill as one uninterrupted scheduling unit, those requests may have to wait for that unit to finish before their next decode step.

Shortening the observation reduces that work. Once the request reaches the server, the remaining question is when the work runs, because the scheduler shares execution time among all admitted requests and need not run a long prefill as one unit. Iteration-level scheduling, which re-forms the batch at every model iteration instead of once per request, made that sharing possible[^fn-iteration-level-scheduling] [@yu2022orca]; splitting prefills into chunks that ride alongside ongoing decodes then bounded how long any one iteration could stall them [@agrawal2023sarathi; @agrawal2024sarathi].

::: {#dfn-chunked-prefill .callout-definition title="Chunked prefill"}

***Chunked prefill***\index{Chunked prefill!definition} is a scheduling policy that splits a request's uncached prompt into token spans processed over several engine iterations, each iteration also advancing ongoing decodes, while preserving causal order.

1. **Significance**: It bounds the gap between output tokens for ongoing requests by one iteration instead of one whole prefill, at the cost of a modestly later first token for the new request.
2. **Distinction**: A chunk is a unit of scheduling, not of storage; the allocator maps the resulting KV state into blocks whose size need not match the chunk.
3. **Common pitfall**: Treating the per-iteration token budget as a time bound. Iteration time also depends on attended context length and batch composition, so the budget must be calibrated against measured gaps between output tokens.

:::

[^fn-iteration-level-scheduling]: **Iteration-Level Scheduling**: Request-level batching fixes a batch until its longest member finishes, so a short request waits for a long one and a new arrival waits for the whole batch. Scheduling at the granularity of one model iteration lets finished requests leave and new ones join between steps [@yu2022orca]. Chunked prefill depends on that granularity: without it, there is no boundary at which a chunk and a set of decodes can be combined. \index{Iteration-level scheduling!chunked prefill}

### Preserving the causal computation

For the causal attention used here, processing a later chunk requires the compatible per-layer KV state for the earlier prefix. Each query in the active chunk can attend to preceding tokens and to its own position, but not to later tokens in that chunk or in the remainder of the prompt. The engine preserves token positions and the causal mask while extending the stored state. It reads earlier keys and values rather than recomputing their projections from the beginning.

Chunking therefore changes the execution schedule and preserves the causal computation, up to floating-point differences across kernels and batch arrangements. It has a cost: later chunks re-read earlier attention state, and smaller steps add scheduling and kernel-launch overhead.

### Choosing how much work to admit

A simple scheduler gives each iteration a **token budget**\index{Token budget!chunked prefill} $C_{\text{budget}}$. With ordinary autoregressive decoding, each selected decode request contributes one new token position, and each selected prefill contributes the number of positions in its next chunk. An iteration that admits prefill chunks of $c_i$ tokens and a set $\mathcal{D}$ of decode requests must satisfy

$$\sum_{i} c_i + |\mathcal{D}| \le C_{\text{budget}}$$ {#eq-kv-token-budget}

and the admitted combination must also fit the available memory. A request whose prompt is only partly processed retains the completed prefix state while waiting for its next iteration.

Suppose the engine first reserves room for ongoing decode requests and then uses the remaining budget for prefill chunks. An existing request can make progress without waiting for another request's entire prompt. The new request, however, may need several iterations to complete its prefill, including waits while other work runs. Giving every iteration to existing decodes would protect them at the expense of new requests; admitting large prefills can reverse that priority. A useful policy must provide both decode responsiveness and eventual progress for prefills.

```{python}
#| label: kv-chunked-iteration-calc
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ CHUNKED PREFILL: STALL VERSUS CHUNK
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-vol3-kvcache-chunked-prefill, paragraph after @eq-kv-token-budget.
# │ Goal: Show the scale of the decode-gap vs. prompt-completion trade.
# │ Show: ~5 ms decode-only step; ~162 ms monolithic prefill; ~22 ms per
# │       512-token chunked iteration; ~173 ms prompt completion; ~8x smaller gap.
# │ How: Weight-only step time max(Nb/beta, 2N tokens/pi) (@eq-appdx-batched-step)
# │      on the node with 16-bit weights; sustained rate from PrefixHit.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_multiple, MarkdownStr

class ChunkedIteration:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
    decodes = 32  # scenario: ongoing decode requests
    prompt_tokens = 4_096  # scenario: new uncached prefill
    chunk_tokens = 512  # scenario: prefill chunk per iteration
    n_params = PrefixHit.n_params
    rate = PrefixHit.sustained_rate
    t_weights = PrefixHit.t_weight_read

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_decode = max(t_weights, (2 * n_params * decodes * flop / rate).to(ms))
    t_mono = max(t_weights, (2 * n_params * prompt_tokens * flop / rate).to(ms))
    gap_mono = t_decode + t_mono
    n_chunks = prompt_tokens // chunk_tokens
    t_iter = max(t_weights, (2 * n_params * (chunk_tokens + decodes) * flop / rate).to(ms))
    t_chunked_done = n_chunks * t_iter
    gap_ratio = (gap_mono / t_iter).to("").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(prompt_tokens % chunk_tokens == 0, "Chunks must tile the prompt")
    check(t_decode == t_weights, "Decode-only step must sit at the weight-read floor")
    check(t_iter > t_weights, "A 544-token iteration must be arithmetic-bound")
    check(t_mono < t_chunked_done < 1.1 * t_mono, "Chunking must delay prompt completion only modestly")
    check(6 < gap_ratio < 9, "Prose claims roughly an eightfold smaller worst gap")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    decodes_str = fmt_int(decodes)
    prompt_str = fmt_int(prompt_tokens)
    chunk_str = fmt_int(chunk_tokens)
    iter_tokens_str = fmt_int(chunk_tokens + decodes)
    n_chunks_str = "eight" if n_chunks == 8 else fmt_int(n_chunks)
    t_decode_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_int(t_decode.magnitude)} ms")
    t_mono_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_int(t_mono.magnitude)} ms")
    gap_mono_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_int(gap_mono.magnitude)} ms")
    t_iter_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_int(t_iter.magnitude)} ms")
    t_done_str = MarkdownStr(f"{fmt_int(t_chunked_done.magnitude)} ms")
    gap_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(gap_ratio))
```

A weight-only estimate still shows the scale of the trade. Apply @eq-appdx-batched-step to the eight-accelerator node with 16-bit weights, counting the token positions that @eq-kv-token-budget admits in one iteration and using the sustained rate assumed for the prefix-hit estimate. With `{python} ChunkedIteration.decodes_str` ongoing decodes and nothing else, each step sits at the weight-read floor of about `{python} ChunkedIteration.t_decode_str`. Admitting a `{python} ChunkedIteration.prompt_str`-token prefill as one unit adds about `{python} ChunkedIteration.t_mono_str` of arithmetic before those decodes run again, so their gap between tokens grows to about `{python} ChunkedIteration.gap_mono_str`. With `{python} ChunkedIteration.chunk_str`-token chunks, each iteration carries `{python} ChunkedIteration.iter_tokens_str` positions and takes about `{python} ChunkedIteration.t_iter_str`. The decodes now advance in each of the `{python} ChunkedIteration.n_chunks_str` iterations, so their worst gap is about `{python} ChunkedIteration.gap_ratio_mult_str` smaller, while the new prompt completes after about `{python} ChunkedIteration.t_done_str` instead of `{python} ChunkedIteration.t_mono_str`. Chunking buys existing streams a much shorter gap for a modest delay in the new request's first token.

@Fig-vol3-chunked-timeline draws both schedules to scale. The estimate omits attention traffic, which grows with each chunk's context, and per-iteration overhead, so measured iterations run longer and the budget must come from measurement.

::: {#fig-vol3-chunked-timeline fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Monolithic vs. Chunked Prefill**: Both timelines use the weight-only estimate, on one time axis, for a `{python} ChunkedIteration.prompt_str`-token prefill arriving while `{python} ChunkedIteration.decodes_str` requests decode. Admitted as one unit (a), the prefill separates two decode tokens by about `{python} ChunkedIteration.gap_mono_str`. Split into `{python} ChunkedIteration.chunk_str`-token chunks (b), every iteration also advances the decodes, so the gap is one iteration of about `{python} ChunkedIteration.t_iter_str`, and the prompt finishes slightly later. Attention traffic and per-iteration overhead, omitted here, would lengthen every bar." fig-alt="Two horizontal timelines on a shared time axis with ticks at 0, 50, 100, and 150 milliseconds. Timeline a has one long prefill bar for 4,096 tokens followed by a short decode step, with output-token markers only at the start and the end and a bracket labeling the gap between decode tokens. Timeline b has eight equal bars labeled chunk 1 to chunk 8 plus decodes, with a token marker at every bar boundary and a bracket over the first bar. Each timeline marks where the prompt completes."}
![](images/svg/chunked_prefill_scheduling_timeline.svg)
:::

We can evaluate the trade-off by replaying the same arrival trace under different budgets. Measure time to first token for newly admitted requests, gaps between generated tokens for ongoing requests, completed useful work, and memory occupancy. Include queueing and scheduling waits in the latency measurements, and examine the slow requests rather than only the average. Client-visible streaming intervals may also include buffering and network delay, so they are not interchangeable with server iteration times.

Smaller chunks offer more frequent scheduling opportunities but delay prompt completion and add overhead. Larger chunks improve execution efficiency while making other requests wait longer. The budget is therefore an operating choice: set it to the largest chunk whose iteration time still meets the inter-token target of the ongoing streams.

### Separating prefill and decode placement {#sec-vol3-kvcache-disaggregated}

Chunking shares execution time on a worker. **Prefill-decode disaggregation**\index{Prefill-decode disaggregation!definition} instead assigns the two phases to different workers, so that their resources and parallelism can be chosen separately [@patel2024; @zhong2024distserve]. The two techniques compose: a separated prefill worker can still process prompts in chunks.

Separation introduces a handoff. The decode worker needs compatible attention state, sufficient destination memory, and an agreed representation before it can continue the request. Transferring that state consumes bandwidth and may require layout conversion; requests can also queue at either worker. Even a direct device-to-device transfer contends for links and memory bandwidth.

The operator therefore compares the latency and capacity of the complete path, including both queues and the handoff, rather than choosing separation from peak link bandwidth alone. For an agent using a hosted endpoint, these placement decisions usually remain inside the serving system. The agent observes their effects through request latency and service limits.

Chunking determines how an active request shares compute. Whether that request's attention state stays on the accelerator while the agent waits for an external tool is a separate memory-management decision, and it begins when generation pauses.

## Paused-State Policies {#sec-vol3-kvcache-swapping}

Return to the earlier integration-test wait, before its log arrives. The serving policy stipulated at the start of this chapter retains the repair's compatible attention state on the accelerator. Once the request no longer needs active computation, the serving operator chooses a **paused-state policy**\index{Paused-state policy!definition}: keep the state, move it elsewhere, or drop it and reconstruct it when needed. Serving research on tool-augmented generation analyzed these same three options, as preserve, swap, and discard, and chose among them per request by the accelerator memory each would waste [@abhyankar2024infercept]. The choice trades accelerator capacity against storage, transfer, and computation at resumption. Memory is a resource bound, and invariant closure places resource bounds in the runtime below the model (principle \ref{pri-invariant-closure}), so the serving system owns the pause decision.

### What can actually be reclaimed

The relevant size is the physical allocation the policy can release. Prefix blocks shared with an active sibling stay allocated after the paused trajectory drops its reference, and a block being read, written, or copied stays unavailable until the operation completes. The uniquely reclaimable storage is what remains, and every pause-policy calculation starts from it.

Moving state requires both space at the destination and a safe handoff. The runtime preserves the source until the copy completes successfully, records where the valid copy resides, and releases only blocks whose remaining ownership and in-flight operations permit reclamation. Before resumption, it must obtain accelerator capacity and make the required state accessible to the attention computation. During copying, source and destination storage can both be occupied. A host-memory budget must include this staging demand as well as already parked trajectories.

Dropping KV loses computation, and it loses no information as long as the inputs survive. Reconstruction needs the exact token sequence and the applicable model, adapter, position, mask, and multimodal configuration; a conversation summary is no substitute. It starts from any compatible prefix still available and processes the rest again. A hosted caller has these choices only as far as the service exposes them.

### Comparing keep, move, and drop
